solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who associate oath changes with major constitutional amendments may place the Third Schedule after the 42nd Amendment, not realising oath formats were original.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets students who know major amendments altered constitutional provisions and assume the Third Schedule (oath formats) was also amended to its present form. Students may misplace it after major amendments because they associate 'what the PM does' with later developments. The sequence test also checks knowledge of Amendment numbers' chronological order.

• The 42nd Amendment is associated with the Emergency period (1975-77) and PM Indira Gandhi.
• The 91st Amendment was enacted following recommendations to prevent unstable, oversized coalition Cabinets.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 78 duties — mandatory nature; 44th Amendment reconsideration clause

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 78(b), the Prime Minister is constitutionally obligated to furnish information to the President upon request — this obligation cannot be waived on grounds of Cabinet confidentiality.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 78(b) uses the word 'shall' — the PM must furnish information the President calls for. Cabinet confidentiality is a constitutional convention but does not override this explicit constitutional duty.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Amendment (1978), the President of India can return advice from the Council of Ministers multiple times before being required to act on it.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment allows the President to return advice ONCE for reconsideration. After reconsideration, the President must act on the advice — multiple returns are not permitted.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 78(c) gives the President the power to require the PM to submit, for CoM consideration, decisions taken by individual ministers without prior Cabinet sanction.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 78(c) explicitly states that if the President so requires, the PM shall submit for CoM consideration any matter on which a minister has acted without prior Cabinet sanction.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who are certain about Statements 1 and 3 may incorrectly assume Statement 2 is also correct, selecting 'all three' without carefully checking the 'multiple times' claim.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 78(b) uses 'shall' — mandatory obligation; Cabinet confidentiality cannot override it. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: The 44th Amendment allows ONE return of advice — not multiple. Statement 2 is incorrect due to 'multiple times'.
Statement 3: Article 78(c) is precisely about requiring PM to submit individual ministerial decisions for CoM consideration — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 extends the 44th Amendment's reconsideration clause from 'once' to 'multiple times'. Students who know the President can return advice (which is the main takeaway) but have not memorised that it is limited to one return will mark Statement 2 as correct. The phrase 'multiple times' is the scope-extension that makes Statement 2 false.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 78 and 74 together define the PM's constitutional communication duties and the limits of Presidential independence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 78(b)'s 'shall' is unconditional. The President is entitled to information and the PM cannot withhold it citing Cabinet confidentiality — these are distinct constitutional obligations.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 44th Amendment (1978) allows the President to return advice ONCE. After the CoM sends back reconsidered advice, the President must act on it — there is no second or third return.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 78(c) is an important but underappreciated provision — it allows the President to require the PM to submit individual ministerial decisions (taken without Cabinet sanction) for collective CoM consideration. This reinforces collective responsibility.

Value Addition:
• Articles 74 and 78 together form the constitutional bridge between the President and the CoM — Article 74 governs the advisory relationship; Article 78 governs the communication duties.
• The one-time reconsideration clause under Article 74 (post-44th Amendment) is the President's only formal mechanism to send advice back.
• Article 78(c) is a check on individual ministerial autonomy — reinforcing collective cabinet decision-making.

solution.concept_anchor: 91st Amendment CoM cap — applies to states too; coalition constraints on PM
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the 91st Amendment caps CoM size may assume the cap is only at 15% of Lok Sabha strength (Union) and does not apply to state Cabinets, making option (b) appear correct.
elimination_logic: The scenario asks about a Chief Minister's ability to expand a state Cabinet beyond the 15% cap, citing PM's prerogative as a comparison.
Eliminate (a): PM's power of portfolio allocation is under Article 77(3) — this doesn't exempt states from the 91st Amendment cap.
Eliminate (b): The 91st Amendment applies uniformly to both Union CoM and state Cabinets — the CM cannot expand beyond 15% of state legislature strength.
Eliminate (c): The 15% cap is calculated on total strength of the state legislative assembly (Vidhan Sabha), not on elected seats — this distinction is not the right calculation basis either.

Confirm (d): The 91st Amendment's 15% cap applies to state Cabinets calculated on total strength of the state Vidhan Sabha. The CM, like the PM, cannot exceed this cap — no exception exists for coalition compulsions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the PM's portfolio allocation power (which is largely unconstrained within the CoM cap) with the question of whether the 91st Amendment's CoM size cap applies to states. Students who know the amendment in the context of Union CoM may not have connected it to state Cabinets. Additionally, 'coalition compulsion' is a practical argument that students might accept as creating constitutional flexibility — it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the scope of the 91st Amendment's CoM size cap and whether coalition politics can override it.

Applicable principle: The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) inserted Article 164(1A), which caps the Council of Ministers of each state at 15% of the total membership of the Legislative Assembly, with a minimum of 12 ministers. This cap applies uniformly — no exception for coalition governments.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The PM's portfolio allocation power (Article 77(3)) governs the Union executive. It does not create an exemption for state Cabinets from the 91st Amendment cap.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 91st Amendment applies to both Union and state Cabinets. A state CM cannot cite inapplicability of the cap — it is constitutionally binding.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 15% cap is indeed on total strength of the state assembly — but this makes the cap MORE constraining than the option suggests (total strength includes vacancies), and the CM cannot circumvent it.
• Option (d) — Correct: The 15% cap applies to all states; coalition compulsions create political difficulty but no constitutional exception. The CM must adhere to the cap regardless.

Value Addition:
• Article 164(1A) (introduced by 91st Amendment) is the constitutional basis for the state CoM cap.
• The minimum floor is 12 ministers even for small states — preventing tiny Cabinets.
• At the Union, the corresponding provision is Article 75(1A) — also inserted by the 91st Amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: H.D. Deve Gowda — PM from Rajya Sabha; no constitutional Acting PM provision
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Manmohan Singh served as PM from the Rajya Sabha (2004-2014) may incorrectly credit Deve Gowda to Lok Sabha, or confuse his House membership.
elimination_logic: Option (a): Article 65 provides for VP acting as President — this is correct and the pair is accurately matched.
Option (b): Manmohan Singh served as PM while being a Rajya Sabha member (2004-2014) — this pair is correctly matched.

Option (c): H.D. Deve Gowda was indeed a PM from the Rajya Sabha (1996-97) — but the pair claims he was 'the first and only PM from the Rajya Sabha'. Manmohan Singh also served from the RS, making this claim factually incorrect.
Option (d): The 91st Amendment applies to states too — this pair is correctly matched.
Confirm (c) as incorrectly matched — Deve Gowda was NOT the only RS PM; Manmohan Singh also served from the RS.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap here uses the phrase 'first and only' to create a false exclusivity. H.D. Deve Gowda was indeed the first PM from the Rajya Sabha but Manmohan Singh subsequently served two full terms (2004-2014) also from the Rajya Sabha. Students who know Deve Gowda was an RS PM may not catch the 'only' qualifier, especially since Deve Gowda is less prominent in public memory than Manmohan Singh.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of which PMs served from the Rajya Sabha and whether a constitutional provision exists for Acting PM.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Article 65 explicitly provides for the Vice President to act as President during a vacancy or disability. This is a constitutional provision, accurately described.
• Option (b) — Correctly matched: Manmohan Singh served as Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014 as a Rajya Sabha member. Both terms were completed from the RS — this pair is accurate.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: H.D. Deve Gowda was the FIRST PM from the Rajya Sabha (1996-97), not the only one. Manmohan Singh subsequently served as a Rajya Sabha PM for ten years, disproving the 'only' claim.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: The 91st Amendment (2003) cap of 15% on CoM size applies to both Union and state governments — this pair is accurate.

Value Addition:
• H.D. Deve Gowda (1996-97) was the first PM to be from the Rajya Sabha.
• Manmohan Singh (2004-2014) served the longest consecutive period as a Rajya Sabha PM.
• The absence of a constitutional 'Acting PM' provision is a notable gap — contrast with Article 65 for VP acting as President.

solution.concept_anchor: PM's advice to President — not absolutely immune from judicial review

statement_analysis.statement: The advice tendered by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers to the President is absolutely immune from judicial review under Article 74(2), which bars courts from examining the content or basis of such advice.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 74(2) does bar courts from inquiring whether advice was tendered and the nature of that advice. However, the question of whether the advice was based on extraneous or mala fide considerations remains constitutionally debated — courts have not definitively declared complete immunity.

statement_analysis.statement: A caretaker Prime Minister, who continues in office after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha pending new elections, loses all constitutional powers and can only take routine administrative decisions as specified by the Election Commission.
statement_analysis.reason: A caretaker PM retains full legal powers under the Constitution. The Election Commission's Model Code of Conduct creates political constraints but the MCC is not law — it does not legally strip the caretaker PM of constitutional powers.

statement_analysis.statement: Anti-defection provisions under the Tenth Schedule do not prevent a political party from issuing a whip directing its members on how to vote in a no-confidence motion against the government.
statement_analysis.reason: Anti-defection law does not prohibit party whips on no-confidence motions. A member who votes against a whip on a no-confidence motion may face disqualification — this is a lawful use of party discipline.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 74(2) bars courts from looking into advice may mark Statement 1 as correct (not 'not correct'), thereby selecting only Statement 2 as the not-correct one.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 74(2) bars inquiry into advice's content, but debates on mala fide/extraneous basis mean absolute immunity is not settled — Statement 1 overstates with 'absolutely immune'. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Caretaker PM retains full legal powers — the MCC is not law. 'Loses all constitutional powers' is a blatant overstatement. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: Anti-defection law allows party whips on no-confidence motions — members must follow the whip or risk disqualification. Statement 3 IS correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are both NOT correct — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses Article 74(2) accurately to its face — courts cannot inquire into advice tendered and its content. But the statement adds 'absolutely immune', which is an overstatement. The judicial review question on mala fide or extraneous considerations is unsettled. Statement 2 targets the common belief that caretaker governments are legally constrained — they are conventionally restrained but legally full-powered. The MCC is not a legal instrument that strips constitutional powers.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision in understanding both the scope of judicial review of executive advice and the legal position of a caretaker PM.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into the advice tendered and its nature — this much is clear. However, whether courts can examine if advice was based on mala fide or extraneous considerations is a live constitutional debate. 'Absolutely immune' overstates the protection.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The caretaker PM retains all constitutional powers. The restraints are conventional — expected political behaviour, not legal obligations. The Election Commission's Model Code of Conduct has no statutory force to strip powers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) does not prevent parties from issuing whips on no-confidence motions. Party discipline on such votes is constitutionally valid.

Value Addition:
• Article 74(2) is one of the constitutional provisions protecting Cabinet confidentiality by barring inquiry into the advice-giving process.
• MCC compliance is enforced by the Election Commission through de-recognition and similar measures, but violations do not automatically invalidate government decisions.
• The whip on no-confidence motions makes the anti-defection law a tool that reinforces coalition discipline at critical moments.

solution.concept_anchor: PMO — non-constitutional; Cabinet Secretariat — Article 77(3) basis

statement_analysis.statement: B.R. Ambedkar described the Prime Minister as 'primus inter pares' — first among equals — reflecting the constitutional design of the Council of Ministers as a collegial body.
statement_analysis.reason: This characterisation reflects the formal constitutional position — all ministers are equal members of the CoM. The PM's dominance evolved through practice rather than being originally designed.

statement_analysis.statement: The Cabinet Secretariat, which coordinates the functioning of the Cabinet and its committees, derives its constitutional basis from Article 77(3) of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 77(3) empowers the President (on PM's advice) to make rules for the conduct of government business — the Cabinet Secretariat operates under these rules and is thus constitutionally anchored in Article 77(3).

statement_analysis.statement: The PMO was created by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment to coordinate the PM's expanded responsibilities following the Emergency period.
statement_analysis.reason: The PMO was not created by any constitutional amendment. It is an executive body established by government order. The 42nd Amendment did not create the PMO.

statement_analysis.statement: The Cabinet Secretary, who heads the Cabinet Secretariat, is senior to the Principal Secretary of the PMO in the official hierarchy of civil servants.
statement_analysis.reason: The Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most IAS officer — higher in civil service hierarchy than the Principal Secretary to the PM. This reflects the formal seniority even though the PMO has gained practical influence.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know PMO is powerful and that Cabinet Secretary is senior may assume all four statements are correct without examining Statement 3's false attribution to the 42nd Amendment.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Ambedkar's 'primus inter pares' characterisation is well-documented — Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Article 77(3) is the constitutional basis for Cabinet Secretariat functioning — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: PMO was NOT created by the 42nd Amendment — it was created by executive order. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most IAS officer — senior to Principal Secretary PMO — Statement 4 is correct.
Statements 1, 2, and 4 correct — 'Only three' — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible fabrication — students know the 42nd Amendment strengthened the PM's office and that the PMO expanded during Indira Gandhi's period. Attributing the PMO's creation to the 42nd Amendment seems plausible because the timing overlaps with Emergency-era centralization. However, the PMO has no constitutional or statutory basis — it was created and expanded through executive orders, not any amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
The PMO-Cabinet Secretariat distinction and the theoretical vs. actual position of the PM within the CoM are critical exam topics.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ambedkar's 'primus inter pares' (first among equals) characterised the PM as constitutionally coordinate with other ministers — dominance evolved through practice, not original design.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 77(3) is the constitutional foundation — it authorises rules for conduct of government business, under which the Cabinet Secretariat operates.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The PMO has no constitutional basis. It was established and has grown through executive orders and government decisions — not the 42nd Amendment or any other amendment.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Cabinet Secretary sits at the apex of the Indian Administrative Service hierarchy — formally senior to the Principal Secretary of the PMO, even as the PMO's political proximity to the PM gives it practical influence.

Value Addition:
• The PMO was institutionalised under Indira Gandhi but its origins pre-date the Emergency as a small secretarial staff attached to the PM.
• Cabinet Secretary coordinates inter-ministerial consultations and Cabinet Committee agendas.
• The tension between PMO (political proximity) and Cabinet Secretariat (hierarchical seniority) reflects the dual nature of India's executive machinery.

solution.concept_anchor: Anti-defection — does not apply to preventing whip on no-confidence vote
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both A and R as factually true may assume R explains A without noticing the directional mismatch — anti-defection enables whip enforcement, not restricts it.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Political parties can issue a whip directing members how to vote in a no-confidence motion; members who defy the whip can be disqualified under the 10th Schedule.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. The anti-defection law does NOT restrict a party from issuing a whip on no-confidence motions. In fact, it reinforces party discipline by making defection from a whip a disqualification ground. R says anti-defection law 'restricts' this — which is the reverse of the truth.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, answer is (c).
Confirm: A is correct, R is incorrect — correct_option is 'c'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here reverses the relationship between anti-defection law and party whips. The anti-defection law (10th Schedule) actually ENABLES parties to enforce whips — defying a valid whip leads to disqualification. The Reason incorrectly states that anti-defection law restricts parties from issuing whips on no-confidence votes. A student who knows both concepts loosely may assume R correctly describes a restriction — without knowing that anti-defection law works in the opposite direction, enforcing party discipline rather than limiting it.
solution.final_explanation:
The 10th Schedule (anti-defection) and no-confidence motions interact in a way that requires careful directional thinking.

Assertion (A): Correct. A political party can issue a whip directing its members on a no-confidence motion. A member who defies the whip can be disqualified under the 10th Schedule for 'voting contrary to the direction issued by the political party'. The anti-defection law thus reinforces party discipline on confidence votes.

Reason (R): Incorrect. The anti-defection law does not restrict parties from issuing whips on no-confidence motions — it does the opposite. It makes compliance with party whips legally enforceable through disqualification. R states the reverse of the actual legal relationship.

Since A is correct but R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Anti-defection disqualification is decided by the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) — their decisions are subject to judicial review.
• The 10th Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985) — often confused with the 91st Amendment.
• A member cannot be disqualified for abstaining from a vote if no valid whip was issued — disqualification requires a valid party direction.

solution.concept_anchor: Prorogation vs. dissolution — different constitutional consequences

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Under Article 85(2), both prorogation of Parliament and dissolution of the Lok Sabha are carried out by the President, but only dissolution terminates the membership of the Lok Sabha — prorogation merely ends a session.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 85(2)(a) provides for prorogation (ending a session) and Article 85(2)(b) for dissolution (ending the House). Members retain their seats through prorogation; dissolution ends the entire House's existence pending new elections.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: If the President refuses a Prime Minister's advice to dissolve the Lok Sabha, the President may personally dissolve the Lok Sabha using residual constitutional discretion without any ministerial advice.
statement_analysis.reason: The President cannot dissolve the Lok Sabha unilaterally. Dissolution requires ministerial advice — the President may refuse one PM's advice but must still act on valid ministerial advice (from a new PM if one can be found). Unilateral Presidential dissolution is constitutionally impermissible.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know prorogation vs. dissolution are different and that the President has discretion may assume both statements are broadly correct without checking Statement 2's specific claim of 'unilateral Presidential dissolution'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Prorogation (Article 85(2)(a)) ends sessions; dissolution (Article 85(2)(b)) ends the House — members lose seats only on dissolution. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 'Personally dissolve using residual constitutional discretion' — the President cannot dissolve LS without ministerial advice under any circumstances. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates Presidential discretion (which allows declining one PM's advice) with an imaginary Presidential power to dissolve the Lok Sabha unilaterally. Presidential discretion in this context means the President can explore alternative government formation — it never means the President can independently dissolve the House. Students who know 'President has discretion on dissolution' may read this as validating Statement 2 without noticing 'without any ministerial advice'.
solution.final_explanation:
The prorogation-dissolution distinction and the limits of Presidential discretion are tested together here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 85(2)(a) is prorogation — ends a parliamentary session, Members retain seats, pending business is held over. Article 85(2)(b) is dissolution — the entire Lok Sabha ceases to exist; all Members lose their seats; pending bills lapse (except those in Rajya Sabha or joint committee).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Presidential discretion in dissolution means the President may decline to immediately dissolve on one PM's advice and explore if another PM can be appointed. It does NOT mean the President can dissolve the Lok Sabha unilaterally without any ministerial advice. Dissolution without advice would violate the parliamentary principle that the President is a constitutional head acting only on advice.

Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse upon dissolution; bills pending in Rajya Sabha or passed by both Houses but pending Presidential assent do not lapse.
• The President's power to prorogue and summon Parliament (Article 85(1)) is exercised on CoM advice.
• A PM can advise prorogation to avoid a no-confidence motion — but this is seen as a constitutional impropriety, not a constitutional right.

solution.concept_anchor: PM chairs Inter-State Council under Article 263
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the President is the constitutional head may assume the President chairs the Inter-State Council, not the PM.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): The President is the constitutional authority who establishes the Inter-State Council under Article 263 — but the PM, not the President, chairs it in practice.
Eliminate (c): The Vice President chairs the Rajya Sabha but has no designated role in the Inter-State Council.
Eliminate (d): The Home Minister is a senior member of the Inter-State Council but does not chair it.
Confirm (a): The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the Inter-State Council under Article 263.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes the President (who constitutionally establishes the Inter-State Council under Article 263) for the PM (who actually chairs it). Students who know Article 263 gives the President power to establish an Inter-State Council may incorrectly assume the President also chairs it. The PM's chairing role is by convention and executive order, not explicitly stated in Article 263 itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The Inter-State Council is one of the key coordination bodies that the PM chairs.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Prime Minister chairs the Inter-State Council. It was established in 1990 by a Presidential Order under Article 263. The PM is the Chairperson; members include Chief Ministers of all states and UTs with Legislatures, and Cabinet Ministers nominated by the PM.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The President establishes the Council under Article 263 but does not chair it. The chairing function belongs to the PM.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Vice President has no designated role in the Inter-State Council.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Home Minister is a member of the Council but does not chair it.

Value Addition:
• Article 263 allows the President to establish an Inter-State Council for investigating and discussing inter-state disputes, coordinating policy, and recommending action.
• The Sarkaria Commission strongly recommended revitalising the Inter-State Council as a forum for Centre-State consultation.
• The Inter-State Council was re-activated in 2016 after a gap of several years — its meetings are significant federal consultative exercises.

solution.concept_anchor: PM's resignation — dissolves CoM not LS; article 75(3) operative protection

statement_analysis.statement: When a Prime Minister resigns, the President is constitutionally required to immediately dissolve the Lok Sabha and call fresh elections.
statement_analysis.reason: When a PM resigns, the Lok Sabha is not automatically dissolved. The President may invite another leader to form the government if an alternative majority is available. Dissolution is one option, not a mandatory consequence.

statement_analysis.statement: The resignation of the Prime Minister automatically results in the vacation of office by all other members of the Council of Ministers.
statement_analysis.reason: Since the CoM is collectively constituted and the PM is its head, the PM's resignation dissolves the entire Council of Ministers. All ministers vacate office when the PM resigns.

statement_analysis.statement: There is no provision in the Constitution that sets a fixed duration after which the Prime Minister must seek a fresh mandate from the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike the President (5-year term) or Rajya Sabha members (6-year terms), the PM has no fixed tenure — the PM continues as long as the Lok Sabha confidence is maintained. No constitutional provision requires periodic confidence votes.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who loosely associate PM's resignation with political collapse may assume all three statements including Statement 1 (about LS dissolution) are correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: PM resignation → immediate dissolution of LS is wrong. President can invite alternative leader. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: PM resignation = CoM dissolution — this is correct; PM is the anchor of the CoM.
Statement 3: No fixed tenure in Constitution — correct; PM serves at LS pleasure, not for a fixed term.
Statements 2 and 3 correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a partial-truth trap — PM resignation does lead to dramatic political consequences and often does precede dissolution, but the Constitution does not mandate immediate dissolution. The President retains discretion to explore alternative government formation. Students who associate PM resignation with election season in their lived experience may assume constitutional compulsion where only political probability exists.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional consequences of a PM's resignation are frequently misunderstood and conflated with political outcomes.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The President is NOT constitutionally required to dissolve the Lok Sabha when a PM resigns. The President may explore whether another leader commands majority support. Dissolution is exercised only when no viable alternative government can be formed.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The PM is the constitutional anchor of the CoM. The PM's resignation dissolves the entire CoM because ministers hold office at the President's pleasure on the PM's advice — when the PM vacates, the entire ministerial structure collapses.
• Statement 3 — Correct: No constitutional provision mandates a fixed interval between confidence votes. The PM continues until LS confidence is lost or voluntarily resigns. This is in contrast to the President's explicit 5-year term.

Value Addition:
• After PM resignation, a caretaker government continues until a new PM is appointed — Article 74 requires a CoM at all times.
• Historical examples: In 1996, H.D. Deve Gowda's resignation led to a new coalition under I.K. Gujral without fresh elections.
• The longest-serving PM Jawaharlal Nehru (1947-1964) served until his death — demonstrating the absence of any fixed term constraint.

With reference to the constitutional consequences of a Prime Minister's resignation and the security of the office, consider the following statements:

1. When a Prime Minister resigns, the President is constitutionally required to immediately dissolve the Lok Sabha and call fresh elections.
2. The resignation of the Prime Minister automatically results in the vacation of office by all other members of the Council of Ministers.
3. There is no provision in the Constitution that sets a fixed duration after which the Prime Minister must seek a fresh mandate from the Lok Sabha.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1 only
(c) 2 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
